subject: Science
title: Year 9 Science Exam 5
intro: You may use a calculator. For longer answers write in full sentences and use key words. Describe = say what happens; Explain = say what happens and why (use because and so); Compare = similarities and differences (use whereas); Evaluate = points for and against, then a justified conclusion. 6-mark questions are marked on how well your ideas link together: plan for a minute, then write about 6 linked points. Show your working for calculations. Relative atomic masses (Aᵣ): H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Al = 27, S = 32, Fe = 56, Cu = 64, Zn = 65.

questions.q: A compound contains 2 aluminium atoms for every 3 oxygen atoms. What is its formula?
questions.ms: B1: Al₂O₃.

questions.q: What is the simplest ratio of carbon atoms to hydrogen atoms in ethane, C₂H₆?
questions.ms: B1: 1 : 3 (divide 2 : 6 by 2).

questions.q: Which metal can be extracted by heating its oxide with carbon?
questions.ms: B1: iron. It is less reactive than carbon; the others are more reactive than carbon.

questions.q:
Copper oxide is heated with carbon: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂
Which substance is oxidised?
questions.ms: B1: carbon. It gains oxygen (C → CO₂). Copper oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced.

questions.q: A catalytic converter changes carbon monoxide into a less harmful gas. Which gas?
questions.ms: B1: carbon dioxide (2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂).

questions.q: How many atoms in total are in one formula unit of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂?
questions.ms: Answer: 9. B1: 1 Ca + 2 N + 6 O = 9 (everything inside the bracket is doubled).

questions.q:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mᵣ) of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃.
ElementHCNOAlSFeCuZn
Relative atomic mass, Aᵣ11214162732566465

Balance these equations. Type them with normal numbers, for example 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.
Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
questions.ms: Answer: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃. B1.

questions.q: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
questions.ms: Answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. B2. B1 for 3CO₂ and 4H₂O correct but O₂ wrong.

questions.q: Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
questions.ms: Answer: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. B1.

questions.q:
In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron oxide to make molten iron:
2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe
Calculate the maximum mass of iron that can be made from 40 g of iron oxide. (g)
questions.ms: Answer: 28 g. M1 for Mᵣ of Fe₂O₃ = 160. M1 for 160 g of Fe₂O₃ makes 2 × 56 = 112 g of Fe (or 40 ÷ 160 = 0.25). A1 for 112 × 40 ÷ 160 = 28 g.

questions.q: In an experiment, only 21 g of iron was collected from 40 g of iron oxide. Calculate the percentage yield. (%)
questions.ms: Answer: 75%. M1 for 21 ÷ 28 × 100. A1 for 75. (Follow through from their answer to 9(a).)

questions.q: Explain why companies that make chemicals want a high percentage yield.
questions.ms: B1: less of the reactants / raw materials are wasted. B1: so it is cheaper / more profitable / more sustainable (less waste to get rid of, fewer natural resources used).

questions.q:
Copper carbonate breaks down when it is heated: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂
Calculate the mass of copper carbonate needed to make 20 g of copper oxide. (g)
questions.ms: Answer: 31 g. M1 for Mᵣ of CuCO₃ = 124 and Mᵣ of CuO = 80. M1 for 80 g of CuO comes from 124 g of CuCO₃ (or 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25). A1 for 124 × 20 ÷ 80 = 31 g.

questions.q:
A student heats some magnesium ribbon in an open crucible. The mass of the solid increases.
Another student heats some copper carbonate in an open boiling tube. The mass of the solid decreases.
Use the idea of conservation of mass to explain both results.
questions.ms: B1: mass is conserved: no atoms are made or destroyed, the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. B1: magnesium reacts with oxygen from the air, and the oxygen atoms are added to the solid (magnesium oxide), so the mass goes up. B1: copper carbonate gives off carbon dioxide gas, which escapes into the air, so the mass of solid left goes down.

questions.q:
Part of the reactivity series (most reactive first): potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, gold.
Which pair of metals can both be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon?
questions.ms: B1: zinc and iron (both below carbon in the reactivity series).

questions.q: Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by heating aluminium oxide with carbon, and describe how it is extracted instead.
questions.ms: B1: aluminium is more reactive than carbon. B1: so carbon cannot take the oxygen away from (reduce) aluminium oxide / cannot displace aluminium. B1: aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide.

questions.q:
Zinc is extracted by heating zinc oxide (ZnO) with carbon. Carbon dioxide is also made.
Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
questions.ms: Answer: 2ZnO + C → 2Zn + CO₂. B1 for correct formulae. B1 for balancing.

questions.q:
A student adds a piece of magnesium to blue iron sulfate solution.
Predict what will happen and write a word equation for the reaction.
questions.ms: B1: magnesium displaces iron because magnesium is more reactive than iron (iron forms, the solution changes colour). B1: magnesium + iron sulfate → magnesium sulfate + iron.

questions.q:
A student heats different masses of copper carbonate and measures the mass of copper oxide left.
Mass of copper carbonate (g)1.242.483.724.966.20
Mass of copper oxide (g)0.781.572.703.143.90

Which mass of copper oxide is anomalous? (g)
questions.ms: Answer: 2.70 g. B1: it does not fit the pattern (about 2.35 g would be expected).

questions.q: Suggest a reason for the anomalous result.
questions.ms: B1: e.g. that sample was not heated for long enough, so some copper carbonate had not broken down / the solid was weighed while still damp or with something else added.

questions.q: Name the independent variable and the dependent variable.
questions.ms: B1: independent variable: mass of copper carbonate. B1: dependent variable: mass of copper oxide.

questions.q: Describe the relationship between the mass of copper carbonate and the mass of copper oxide. Use data from the table.
questions.ms: B1: as the mass of copper carbonate increases, the mass of copper oxide increases / they are (directly) proportional. B1: data, e.g. doubling 1.24 g to 2.48 g roughly doubles the copper oxide from 0.78 g to 1.57 g.

questions.q: The theoretical yield of copper oxide from 6.20 g of copper carbonate is 4.00 g. Calculate the percentage yield. (%)
The student repeats each test three times and calculates a mean. Why?
options: To make it a fair test
To spot anomalies and reduce the effect of random errors
questions.ms: B1: to spot anomalies and reduce the effect of random errors (makes results more repeatable).

questions.q:
Molten (melted) sodium chloride can be broken down by electrolysis.
Explain why the sodium chloride must be molten, and name the product formed at each electrode.
questions.ms: B1: sodium chloride is an ionic compound / made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. B1: when molten the ions are free to move (in a solid they are fixed), so it can conduct electricity. B1: sodium forms at the negative electrode (cathode), because positive Na⁺ ions are attracted to it. B1: chlorine (gas) forms at the positive electrode (anode).

questions.q:
All new petrol cars must have a catalytic converter.
Evaluate the use of catalytic converters in cars.
questions.ms: 6 marks, level-marked. A Level 3 answer gives points for and against and a justified conclusion. Level 3 (5-6 marks): a detailed, logically linked answer covering most points. Level 2 (3-4 marks): several relevant points, some linked. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, separate statements. Indicative content: FOR: change carbon monoxide (toxic) into carbon dioxide; change nitrogen oxides (cause acid rain, breathing problems) into nitrogen; change unburnt hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water; improve air quality and health in cities; the catalyst is not used up, so it lasts a long time; honeycomb shape gives a large surface area, so reactions are fast. AGAINST: they still produce carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that causes climate change; they use rare, expensive metals (platinum, rhodium, palladium) that must be mined; they only work well when hot, so not on short journeys; they can be stolen. CONCLUSION: e.g. worth using because they greatly reduce toxic gases, although they do not solve climate change.
